misconceptions.description: Believing the page heading <h1> controls the browser tab text rather than the <title> element in <head>
misconceptions.trigger: learner edits <h1> expecting the browser tab to change
misconceptions.feedback: The tab text comes from <title> inside <head>. <h1> is the visible heading on the page. They are two different elements with two different jobs.

misconceptions.description: Assuming the first CSS rule always wins when in fact, at equal specificity, the later rule in source order overrides the earlier one
misconceptions.trigger: learner predicts the earlier color for two same-specificity rules
misconceptions.feedback: At equal specificity the cascade takes the last matching rule. Reorder the rules or raise specificity if you need a different one to win.

misconceptions.description: Pasting AI-generated CSS without checking that its selectors match classes and elements that actually exist in the HTML
misconceptions.trigger: learner applies AI CSS that targets a non-existent class and is surprised nothing changes
misconceptions.feedback: A selector only styles elements it matches. Confirm every class in the CSS exists in your HTML, then keep, add, or drop classes so the two agree.

misconceptions.description: Treating the alt attribute on images as decorative or optional rather than as the accessible description a screen reader announces
misconceptions.trigger: learner ships an with no alt or an empty alt for a meaningful image
misconceptions.feedback: Give meaningful images a short, specific alt describing what they show. That is how non-visual users receive the same information sighted users get.
